paragraphs.heading: What gneiss is
paragraphs.text: Gneiss is a common and widespread kind of metamorphic rock. It forms when high-temperature, high-pressure metamorphic processes act on formations of igneous or sedimentary rock. The pressures range from 2 to 15 kbar, sometimes more, and the temperatures are over 300 °C. Gneiss nearly always has a banded texture, with darker and lighter bands alternating.

paragraphs.heading: How geologists define it
paragraphs.text: In the traditional usage of English and North American geologists, gneiss means a coarse-grained metamorphic rock: its mineral grains are easy to see with the unaided eye. The grains form obvious layers of differing composition, yet the rock has only a weak tendency to break along those layers. In Europe the term has been used more widely, for any coarse, mica-poor, high-grade metamorphic rock.

paragraphs.heading: Dark bands and light bands
paragraphs.text: The minerals in gneiss are arranged in layers, which show up as bands in cross section. This is called gneissic banding. Darker bands have relatively more mafic minerals, those with more magnesium and iron. Lighter bands hold relatively more felsic minerals. Feldspar and quartz are examples, and such minerals are richer in lighter elements like aluminium, sodium and potassium.

paragraphs.heading: How the bands form
paragraphs.text: The banding develops at high temperature when the rock is squeezed more strongly in one direction than in others. Bands form at right angles to the direction of greatest compression, as rotation or recrystallization turns platy minerals into parallel layers. A common cause of this uneven stress is extreme shearing force on the original rock. Shearing is a sliding force, like pushing the top of a deck of cards one way and the bottom the other way. These forces stretch the rock out like a plastic, and the original material is spread into sheets.

paragraphs.heading: Other routes to banding
paragraphs.text: Some banding comes from an original rock made of alternating layers of lighter sandstone and darker shale. Under extreme temperature and pressure these are metamorphosed into bands of quartzite and mica. Another cause is metamorphic differentiation, in which chemical reactions separate different materials into different layers. That process is not fully understood.

paragraphs.heading: Naming a gneiss
paragraphs.text: Many different kinds of rock can be turned into gneiss, so geologists take care to add the colour and mineral composition to the name of any gneiss. An orthogneiss is derived from an igneous rock, while a paragneiss is derived from a sedimentary rock. Augen gneiss, named from the German word for eyes, comes from the metamorphism of granite. It contains elliptic or lens-shaped grains, normally feldspar, surrounded by finer-grained material that deforms around the more resistant feldspar.

paragraphs.heading: Very old rock
paragraphs.text: Continental shields are the stable cores of continents, where ancient rock is exposed, and gneisses are common in their ancient crust. Gneisses, the Acasta Gneiss among them, include some of the oldest rocks on Earth. Gneiss domes are common in orogenic belts, which are regions of mountain formation.
